t: Human origins, archaeology and Stone Age classification
d: Use this group to distinguish changes in technology and subsistence from rigid calendar boxes. The same tool traditions may persist for different lengths of time in different environments.
part: Indian History · PART I — PREHISTORY AND PROTOHISTORY

p: c. 2 million years ago onward (broad South Asian Palaeolithic record)
d: Lower Palaeolithic tools and landscapes; exact earliest dates vary by site and dating method.

p: c. 1.5 million years ago (reported for Attirampakkam-related evidence)
d: Important for discussions of the antiquity of tool-making in India; site-specific dates require careful reading.

p: c. 2 million–300,000 years ago (broad, regionally variable)
d: Hand-axes, cleavers, choppers and flakes; quarry sites, river terraces and open-air localities; study the Soan valley, Narmada basin, Hunsgi-Baichbal and Attirampakkam.
Flake tools and prepared-core techniques; raw materials and methods vary regionally, with evidence from the Narmada, Son, Belan and other river valleys.
Blade tools, burins, bone/antler use in some contexts and varied symbolic behaviour; dates vary by region and cave/rock-shelter context.
Microliths; hunting, fishing, gathering, seasonal mobility and some semi-sedentary settlements.

p: c. 10,000–6000 BCE and later by region
d: Bhimbetka rock shelters, Bagor, Langhnaj, Adamgarh and other sites; association of art and occupation layers must be assessed archaeologically.

t: Neolithic beginnings at Mehrgarh (in today’s Pakistan)
d: Early farming, herding, mud-brick houses and village settlement in the north-western region.
Crops, cattle/sheep/goats, storage, craft specialisation and changing settlement patterns.

t: Neolithic traditions in Kashmir, the Ganga valley, eastern India and the south
d: Dates, crops, pottery and burial patterns differ by region.
Ash mounds, cattle keeping, ground-stone axes and settlements in parts of Karnataka, Andhra and adjoining regions.
Copper artefacts coexist with stone tools; study Ahar-Banas, Malwa, Jorwe, Kayatha and eastern Indian traditions.
South-eastern Rajasthan, copper use, distinctive pottery, farming and settlement networks.
Central and western Deccan farming settlements, pottery and regional exchange; chronological brackets differ by site.
Iron technology spread unevenly; avoid treating the arrival of iron as a single India-wide event.
Stone circles, dolmens, cists, menhirs, cairns and grave goods, particularly across peninsular India.
Iron, black-and-red ware, cattle and rice/millet agriculture, trade and emerging chiefdoms; not a single uniform culture.
Stratigraphy, typology, radiocarbon dating, archaeobotany, zooarchaeology, palaeoclimate, epigraphy and scientific analysis help establish chronology.

t: Harappan / Indus Civilisation: early, mature and late phases
d: “Indus Civilisation” and “Harappan Civilisation” are both used. Its distribution extended beyond the Indus valley into present-day Pakistan and north-western/western India. The script remains undeciphered; therefore, political structure, language and religious interpretation remain open questions.
part: Indian History · PART I — PREHISTORY AND PROTOHISTORY

d: A regional antecedent to later north-western developments, not itself a Harappan city.

t: Ravi / Hakra-related early settlement phase at Harappa and neighbouring regions
d: Village and craft traditions develop before mature urbanism.
Fortified settlements, craft production and wider regional interaction intensify.
Planned cities, standardised weights, seals, drainage, craft specialists and extensive exchange networks.
Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Ganweriwala, Kalibangan, Lothal and other sites; each has a distinct local history.
Street layouts, public and domestic wells, drainage, baked and mud brick, platforms, reservoirs and differentiated settlement sectors.
Wheat, barley, pulses, sesame, cotton evidence, regional rice/millet use, irrigation and floodplain adaptation; crop patterns differed across sites.
Cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats, pigs, dogs and other fauna; horse evidence and its interpretation require caution.
Bead-making, shell work, faience, ceramics, metalworking, stone drilling, bangles, ivory/bone and specialised workshops.
Standardised weight systems support exchange and administration; their exact use in market and state settings is studied archaeologically.
Short inscriptions, animal motifs, sealings and administrative/identity functions; no generally accepted decipherment exists.
Exchange with regions of Afghanistan, Iran, the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia; Meluhha appears in Mesopotamian sources, though identification details are debated.
Copper/bronze, gold, silver and lead; no widespread iron technology in mature Harappan levels.
Painted ceramics, terracotta objects, stone sculpture, ornaments and iconic objects often interpreted cautiously.
Settlement hierarchy, craft and trade networks, public works and signs of coordination; no single uncontested model of kingship or empire.
Shifting river systems, monsoon variability, regional economic changes and changing trade are investigated as contributing factors, not a single proven cause.
Large cities lose population or reorganise, urban standards change and regional cultures become more prominent.
Settlement shifts, changing pottery and craft networks; transformation differed from region to region rather than occurring as one sudden collapse.

t: Railway-era brick removal and later archaeological recognition
d: Harappa’s ancient bricks were reused before the civilisation was properly recognised.
Modern archaeological work establishes the scale of the civilisation; Daya Ram Sahni, R. D. Banerji and John Marshall are central names in the early discovery narrative.
Language, script, religion, social hierarchy, political authority, water management, environmental change and the relationship between Harappan and later communities.

t: Evidence, chronology and historians: how early Indian history is reconstructed
d: This source-focused group preserves the uploaded outline’s emphasis on the construction of history. Keep primary evidence distinct from later interpretation.
part: Indian History · PART I — PREHISTORY AND PROTOHISTORY

d: Sites, artefacts, architecture, botanical/animal remains, burials, settlement pattern, stratigraphy and scientific dating.
Undeciphered Harappan signs differ from later readable inscriptions; inscriptional evidence becomes especially important from the early historic period.
Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads, epics, Buddhist and Jain texts, grammar, political treatises and regional literature; texts have layered compositional histories.
Greek, Roman, Chinese, Tibetan, Persian and Arab accounts; each must be read in the context of its author, aims and access to information.
Ashokan inscriptions are foundational evidence for royal communication, ethical policy, administration and geography.
Punch-marked, Indo-Greek, Shaka, Kushan, Satavahana, Gupta, regional and Sultanate/Mughal coinage; chronology, economic networks and political authority can be inferred cautiously.
Faxian and Xuanzang provide accounts of monasteries, routes, institutions and political/social life; they were not neutral surveys of every region.
Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta, Amir Khusrau, Babur, Abul Fazl and others offer valuable but situated perspectives.

t: Asiatic Society of Bengal founded by William Jones and colleagues
d: A landmark in the institutional study of Asian languages and history, though early Orientalist scholarship also reflected colonial assumptions.

t: James Mill’s *The History of British India*
d: Influential periodisation and colonial interpretation; must be studied critically rather than treated as neutral fact.
Decipherment of Brahmi by James Prinsep (1830s), systematic inscriptions and survey work expand historical evidence.
R. C. Majumdar, D. D. Kosambi, R. S. Sharma, K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, Jadunath Sarkar, Romila Thapar, Irfan Habib, Satish Chandra, Bipan Chandra and others; approaches differ by evidence and method.
Political, social, economic, Marxist, subaltern, feminist, environmental, regional, postcolonial and material-culture approaches; compare arguments and evidence, not names alone.

t: Vedic period: Early / Rigvedic and Later Vedic phases
d: Study the Vedic age through texts, language, ritual, social structure, geography, economy and political institutions. “Arya” and the question of origins are debated; avoid presenting a single migration or homeland theory as settled fact.
rel: Political Economy, Economic Thought and Ideologies
Human Geography — 22. Human Economy and Occupational Structure
part: Indian History · PART II — ANCIENT INDIA

d: Rigveda’s oldest layers; pastoral wealth, cattle, clans, chiefs, assemblies and sacrificial religion are prominent themes.
North-western subcontinent and rivers mentioned in the Rigveda; precise matching of every ancient river-name remains debated.
Jana, chiefs/rajas, assemblies often identified as sabha and samiti, kin networks and warfare; terminology and actual institutional roles are debated.
Household, kinship, gender roles, varna concepts in early form and the importance of cattle; avoid projecting later caste arrangements unchanged into this period.
Pastoralism with agriculture, exchange, gifts, cattle wealth, chariots and metal use; regional variation matters.
Increasing eastward settlement into the Ganga-Yamuna region and expanding importance of agriculture.
Later Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas and early Upanishadic thought; ritual specialists and more stratified social/political institutions.
Iron objects appear in some regions; clearing, farming and settlement expansion help support larger communities.
Early regional state formation and ritual-political traditions in north India.
Inquiry into brahman, atman, knowledge, rebirth and liberation; texts were composed and transmitted over time.

t: Vedic textual layers and oral transmission
d: Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads, Vedangas and later Shrauta/Grihya traditions; do not treat all works as composed simultaneously.
Growth of towns, iron use, coinage, trade and new intellectual/religious movements provide the bridge to the Mahajanapada age.

t: Second urbanisation, Mahajanapadas and the rise of Magadha
d: The “second urbanisation” refers to the growth of cities and states in the Ganga valley and other areas after the Harappan urban phase. Sixteen Mahajanapadas are listed in Buddhist traditions, but the political map changed over time.
rel: Human Geography — 33. Urbanisation: World Patterns and India
part: Indian History · PART II — ANCIENT INDIA

d: Settlements and towns expand in the middle Ganga valley; iron use, rice agriculture, trade, punch-marked coins and urban crafts become important.
Anga, Magadha, Kasi, Kosala, Vajji, Malla, Chedi, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, Matsya, Surasena, Assaka/Asmaka, Avanti, Gandhara and Kamboja.
Varied political forms, including monarchies and oligarchic/clan-based assemblies; do not equate all gana-sanghas automatically with modern democracy.
Fertile alluvial lands, river transport, iron resources in nearby regions, strategic centres, elephants and capable rulers are among the explanatory factors.
Bimbisara expands Magadha through conquest, diplomacy and marriage alliances; Rajagriha/Rajgir is an early centre.
Associated with conflict against Vajji and expansion of Magadhan power; accounts of military innovations require source criticism.
Traditionally associated with the shift of the capital to Pataliputra; precise details vary among sources.
Later rulers, including Anuruddha, Munda and Nagadasaka in some lists; chronology and succession are imperfectly documented.
Shishunaga and Kakavarna/Kalasoka; Magadhan political consolidation continues.
Mahapadma Nanda is the most prominent early ruler in later tradition; Dhana Nanda is the ruler associated with the eve of the Mauryan takeover.
Key rivals and regional powers; rulers and alliances change, and not every succession is securely reconstructed.
Taxes, armies, fortified capitals, merchants, guilds, craft production, urban labour, household structures and varied legal norms.

t: Jain and Buddhist teachings take shape
d: Renunciation, ethics, karma, rebirth and liberation become central intellectual themes alongside Brahmanical traditions.

t: Achaemenid Persian expansion into parts of the north-west
d: Relevant to frontier political and cultural contacts; the precise extent and administrative reach in South Asia are debated.
Battles and alliances in the Indus region; Alexander fought Porus near the Hydaspes/Jhelum in 326 BCE, then his troops refused to advance farther east.
Alexander defeats Porus in a hard-fought battle; Porus is retained as a local ruler/allied king in ancient accounts.
His departure from the region creates a changing political setting for Chandragupta Maurya’s rise.

t: Jainism, Buddhism and other heterodox traditions
d: These traditions arose in a setting of urban growth, debate over ritual authority, renunciation and competing ideas about ethical conduct and liberation. Their biographies and dates come from texts composed and transmitted over time; traditional dates should not be confused with securely fixed contemporary records.
part: Indian History · PART II — ANCIENT INDIA

d: The 24th Tirthankara in Jain tradition; renunciation, austerity, non-violence and disciplined conduct form central teachings. Traditional dates 599–527 BCE are not universally accepted by modern historians.
Jiva and ajiva, karma, liberation, ahimsa, anekantavada, aparigraha and vows; details vary between Digambara and Svetambara traditions.
Monastic and lay communities, oral transmission and later canonical redaction; Ardhamagadhi/Prakrit traditions are important.
Life traditionally centred on birth, renunciation, awakening at Bodh Gaya, first sermon at Sarnath and death/parinirvana at Kushinagar; exact chronology remains disputed.
Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, dependent origination, impermanence, non-self and nirvana; traditions interpret and elaborate these concepts differently.
Sangha, monks and nuns, lay donors, pilgrimage places and oral preservation of teachings.
Rajagriha, Vaishali and later councils in differing sectarian accounts; dates, locations and the number of councils are not identical in all traditions.
Ajivikas, materialist/Lokayata traditions and other teachers known through fragmentary or rival accounts.

t: Jainism and Buddhism in relation to Brahmanical traditions
d: Debate and exchange over sacrifice, caste, karma, rebirth, monasticism, kingship and ethical authority.
Inscriptions refer to dhamma and Buddhist sites/tradition, but the precise relationship between royal dhamma and later Buddhist institutional narratives must be handled carefully.
Pali canon and other early textual collections are compiled/transmitted across extended periods; do not assign a single date to all canonical texts.
Mahayana traditions become increasingly visible; Abhidharma and other schools develop in different regions and at different rates.
Sites such as Nalanda and later Vikramashila attract scholars; institutions evolve over centuries.

t: Jain art, temples and monastic centres
d: Mathura, Karnataka, Gujarat, Rajasthan and other regions develop varied Jain artistic and intellectual traditions.

t: Changing patronage and regional religious landscapes
d: Buddhism declines in many parts of India but persists in Himalayan, eastern and other pockets; explanations are multiple, not a single-cause story.

t: Modern Buddhist and Jain revivals and scholarship
d: Archaeological discovery, textual study, reform movements and new communities reshape how these traditions are understood.

The Mauryan Empire (c. 321–185 BCE) was a major early imperial formation. Inscriptions, Greek accounts, archaeology and later literary works provide different kinds of evidence; the famous *Arthashastra* has a complex textual history and should not be treated as a simple contemporary administrative manual in every detail.
rel: Mauryan and Post-Mauryan Art and Architecture
part: Indian History · PART II — ANCIENT INDIA

d: Defeats the Nanda regime and consolidates power in north India; associated in later sources with Chanakya/Kautilya.
Conflict followed by a settlement involving territories and diplomatic exchange; Megasthenes later serves as a Seleucid envoy at the Mauryan court.
Imperial consolidation, capital at Pataliputra and a large administrative/military apparatus; the extent of direct control varied across the subcontinent.
Continues expansion and imperial rule; details of his campaigns are less securely known than those of Chandragupta and Ashoka.

p: c. 268/265–232 BCE (commonly used range; accession debated)
d: Prominent Mauryan emperor whose inscriptions document dhamma, governance, moral exhortation and communication across a wide realm.

p: c. 261 BCE (traditional event date; some uncertainty)
d: Ashokan inscriptions describe remorse at the suffering caused; war and its aftermath are central to debates on imperial violence and ethical kingship.
Major rock edicts, minor rock edicts, pillar edicts and inscriptions at frontier and regional sites; study Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts, language choices and locations.
Provincial centres, officers, royal inspection, taxation, roads, military logistics and relations with local elites; the system was neither identical everywhere nor fully visible from one text.
Agriculture, state revenues, craft guilds, trade, forests, mining, roads, urban centres, labour and social differentiation.
Polished stone pillars, animal capitals, stupas, caves and royal inscriptions; not all surviving structures can be securely assigned to one ruler.
Ashokan inscriptions refer to Buddhist pilgrimage and dhamma; traditions speak of missions beyond the empire, although narratives need source comparison.
Central authority eventually weakens; succession and the speed of territorial fragmentation are not fully documented.
Dasharatha, Samprati (in Jain tradition), Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan and Brihadratha appear in later lists; sequence and reign dates vary.
Brihadratha is killed by his commander Pushyamitra, traditionally marking the rise of the Shungas.

t: Post-Mauryan India: northern and north-western dynasties
d: Following Mauryan decline, the subcontinent was governed by overlapping regional houses. “Foreign” and “indigenous” are convenient older textbook labels but can oversimplify migration, intermarriage, political integration and cultural exchange.
rel: Mauryan and Post-Mauryan Art and Architecture
part: Indian History · PART II — ANCIENT INDIA

d: Pushyamitra Shunga and Agnimitra are prominent; later rulers are named differently across sources. Study political succession, Sanskrit texts, stupa development and religious patronage without assuming simple, uniform persecution or patronage.
Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana and Susarman; short-lived succession and limited evidence.
Demetrius, Menander/Milinda, Antialcidas and other rulers in the north-west; bilingual coinage, Hellenistic imagery and political interaction.
Associated with the *Milindapanha* tradition; date, political reach and the relationship between the text and historical king require caution.
Maues, Azes and successors rule parts of the north-west and western India; coinage is a key evidence source.
Nahapana and Rudradaman I are prominent; Rudradaman’s Junagadh inscription is a major Sanskrit inscriptional source.
Gondophares and other rulers; political reach is reconstructed chiefly from coinage and limited inscriptions.
Kujula Kadphises consolidates power; Vima Kadphises expands monetary and trade networks.
Major Kushan ruler associated with Central Asian links, Buddhist patronage, monumental art and political expansion; the older 78 CE accession theory is disputed.
Later Kushan rulers sustain regional influence, with changing territorial and economic conditions.
Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical sculpture develops in distinct but interacting regional styles.
Roman, Arabian, Persian Gulf and Southeast Asian connections; ports, textiles, spices, beads and coin flows contribute to urban economies.
Merchants, monks, monasteries and political patrons connect north-western South Asia with wider Eurasia.

t: Post-Mauryan India: Deccan, Kalinga and Sangam south
d: This phase must be studied regionally. Satavahana chronology and ruler order are debated; early Tamil poems illuminate the Chera, Chola and Pandya worlds, but the literary corpus was transmitted and compiled over time.
rel: Mauryan and Post-Mauryan Art and Architecture
part: Indian History · PART II — ANCIENT INDIA

d: Simuka, Satakarni I, Gautamiputra Satakarni, Vasisthiputra Pulumavi and Yajna Sri Satakarni are among the most prominent rulers; succession lists and reign dates remain debated.
Prominent Satavahana ruler known from inscriptions and coinage; associated with conflict against Western Kshatrapas and restoration of Satavahana power.
Prakrit inscriptions, land grants, merchants, guilds, Buddhist cave patronage, coinage and trade across the Deccan.
Kharavela is the best-known ruler, represented by the Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri; inscriptional interpretation is contested in details.

p: c. 300 BCE–300 CE (broad, overlapping literary chronology)
d: Chera, Chola and Pandya ruling houses, chiefs, warfare, poetry, trade and gift exchange.
Rulers such as Nedum Cheralathan and Senguttuvan are prominent in Tamil literary tradition; the precise dating and historicity of individual episodes are debated.
Karikala Chola is the best-known traditional ruler, associated in literature with warfare and irrigation projects; individual claims require literary source criticism.
Rulers at Madurai are associated with the Tamil literary and trade world; inscriptions and texts are not always easily matched to named rulers.
Ettuthokai, Pattuppattu, Tolkappiyam and later compilations; study genre, language, landscape poetics and the difference between literary memory and administrative records.
Muziris, Arikamedu and other coastal sites connect southern India with Mediterranean and Indian Ocean exchange; identifications and routes vary by source.
Agriculture, pastoralism, chiefs, kinship, warfare, bards, merchants, crafts, coastal exchange and differentiated ecological zones.
Jain, Buddhist, Brahmanical and local traditions coexist; inscriptions, cave monuments and literary references show diverse patronage.

t: Gupta Empire, Vakatakas and classical-era developments
d: The term “Golden Age” appears in older historiography but is not a neutral description of life for all groups or regions. Study the political, cultural, scientific and economic record alongside social hierarchy, regional variation and the limits of surviving evidence.
part: Indian History · PART II — ANCIENT INDIA

d: Early Gupta ancestor; evidence for the earliest rulers is limited.
Early dynasty; details of reign and territorial reach are uncertain.
Expansion and matrimonial alliance with the Licchavis; use of the Gupta era is associated with the dynasty’s growing power.
Expansion documented by the Prayaga/Allahabad pillar inscription; the account distinguishes direct annexation, tributary rulers and frontier powers.
Gupta power reaches a high point; the western campaign against Shakas, trade and cultural patronage are key topics.

t: Faxian / Fa Xian travels in India
d: Chinese Buddhist pilgrim describes religious institutions and aspects of society; his itinerary did not cover the whole subcontinent.
Consolidation and continued Gupta coinage, administration and religious patronage.
Defends Gupta power against Huna incursions and faces fiscal/political pressures.
Purugupta, Kumaragupta II, Budhagupta, Narasimhagupta Baladitya and others are known from varying records; sequence, co-rulership and regional authority can be difficult to disentangle.
Imperial centre, provinces, local authorities, land grants, officials, military forces and variable degrees of direct control.
Agriculture, land revenue, trade networks, guilds, coinage and the changing circulation of gold and copper coins.
Family, caste and jati, landholding, legal texts, urban/rural difference, women’s status and the limits of prescriptive literature as evidence for actual life.
Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions, Buddhism, Jainism and local cults; royal identities do not imply exclusive religious practice.
Kalidasa and other writers are associated with the broad classical literary environment; exact personal dates and court links are not always secure.
Major work in mathematics and astronomy; Indian mathematical and astronomical traditions include earlier and later developments too.
Temple forms, sculpture, murals and Buddhist monuments; the category covers regional workshops rather than one uniform “Gupta style”.
Vindhyashakti, Pravarasena I, Rudrasena I, Prithivishena I, Rudrasena II, Prabhavatigupta as regent, Pravarasena II, Narendrasena and later rulers; chronology differs by branch.
Prabhavatigupta’s regency illustrates dynastic alliance and women’s political roles.
Caves developed over time; patronage, cave chronology and the identity of donors are subjects of detailed art-historical study.
Huna pressure, regional assertion, succession and fiscal changes contribute; avoid single-cause explanations.

t: Six classical schools of Indian philosophy
d: Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta are standard groupings; texts and schools develop over long periods.

t: Transition into early medieval regional orders
d: Post-Gupta polities emerge at different times across north, east, Deccan and south India.

t: Post-Gupta north India, Kashmir and Himalayan regions
d: This group covers the shift from Gupta-era imperial structures toward regional kingdoms, including the Pushyabhutis, Maukhari and later northern houses, as well as Kashmir’s powerful dynasties.
part: Indian History · PART III — EARLY MEDIEVAL INDIA

t: Hunas / Alchon Huns and north-western pressures
d: Campaigns and settlements affect parts of north India; names in the sources are complex and should not be collapsed into one undifferentiated “Huna” group.
Ishanavarman and successors; political competition with other north Indian houses.
A distinct eastern line, not simply the same as the earlier imperial Guptas.
Gujarat/Saurashtra dynasty with important centres of learning and land-grant evidence.
Prabhakaravardhana is an important predecessor in the family’s rise.
Major north Indian ruler, patron and author attributed in literary tradition; his authority was powerful but not an uninterrupted rule over all India.
Documents Buddhist institutions, routes and political/geographic information; his account is a source to analyse, not a census.
No simple empire-wide successor; rival houses and regional lineages expand.
Durlabhavardhana, Durlabhaka, Chandrapida, Tarapida and Lalitaditya Muktapida are among the rulers; succession chronology varies.
Prominent Kashmir king; accounts of far-reaching conquests require caution because some are known through later narrative sources.
Avantivarman and successors; irrigation/agrarian development is a key topic.

t: Lohara dynasty and later Kashmir kings
d: Political instability and shifting regional alliances; *Rajatarangini* by Kalhana (12th century) is an important but literary historical source.
Nepalese Licchavis and successors, western Himalayan kingdoms and local ruling houses; each requires regional study rather than being treated as peripheral.

t: Tripartite struggle and the north/east Indian empires
d: The struggle for Kannauj among the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas was a long series of contests, not one continuous three-sided battle. Each dynasty governed different territories and interacted with many subordinate powers.
part: Indian History · PART III — EARLY MEDIEVAL INDIA

d: Nagabhata I is associated with resistance to Arab expansion and early consolidation in western/north-western India.
Gopala is traditionally chosen by regional elites; this is often discussed as an unusual form of ruler selection, though evidence is not exhaustive.
Expands Pala influence into northern India and is involved in the Kannauj contest.
Pala expansion and Buddhist patronage; Nalanda and other monasteries connect regional power to trans-Asian networks.
Campaigns northward as part of the contest among major powers.
Rashtrakuta power extends across wide regions, though political claims and direct control must be distinguished.
Prominent Rashtrakuta ruler known for long reign, literary/cultural patronage and political consolidation.
Leading Gurjara-Pratihara ruler; strengthens the dynasty and is a major figure in north Indian political history.
Continuation of Pratihara authority and influence in north India.
Mahipala I (c. 988–1038, approximate) restores parts of Pala authority; later rulers oversee regional decline.
Final major expansion phase, including campaigns in southern India.
Regional powers such as the Chahamanas, Paramaras, Chandellas and Kalachuris gain autonomy.
Vijayasena, Ballalasena and Lakshmanasena are prominent; the Ganga delta and Bengal’s political order evolve.
Kokalla and other rulers; central Indian political networks and temple patronage.

t: Western Ganga dynasty in southern Karnataka
d: Durvinita and later rulers; Jain patronage and regional ties are important.
Dynastic links with the Cholas and regional succession politics.
Tailapa II, Someshvara I, Vikramaditya VI and later rulers; Deccan competition and court culture.
Provide evidence for village assemblies, temples, agrarian expansion, local elites, taxes and military service.

t: Deccan and southern kingdoms before and during the Chola high period
d: Southern Indian history is not a mere appendix to north Indian chronology. Chalukya, Pallava, Rashtrakuta, Pandya, Chera/Kerala, Chola, Hoysala, Kakatiya and Yadava histories overlap through wars, temples, ports and marriage alliances.
rel: Temple Architecture: Nagara, Dravida and Vesara
part: Indian History · PART III — EARLY MEDIEVAL INDIA

d: Pulakeshin I is associated with the dynasty’s early consolidation.
Prominent Chalukya king who checked Harsha’s southward expansion, fought the Pallavas and became a central figure in Deccan history.
Defeats Chalukya power in one phase of the rivalry and captures Vatapi/Badami in c. 642; later campaigns continue the conflict.
Mahendravarman I, Narasimhavarman I, Paramesvaravarman I, Narasimhavarman II/Rajasimha and successors; Kanchipuram, rock-cut and structural temples are key topics.
Karnataka state formation, inscriptions and temple-centred institutions.
Dantidurga, Krishna I (associated with the Kailasa temple at Ellora), Govinda III, Amoghavarsha I, Indra III and Krishna III are prominent in the succession.

t: Eastern Ganga and other Odisha polities
d: Regional state formation precedes the later Ganga empire and temple-building traditions.
Vijayalaya takes Thanjavur; Aditya I and Parantaka I consolidate the dynasty’s early expansion.
Expands Chola influence, strengthens administration and maritime power, and commissions the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur (completed c. 1010).
Extends campaigns northward and overseas; the Gangaikondacholapuram capital/temple complex commemorates imperial ambition.

t: Chola naval campaign toward Kadaram / Srivijaya-linked centres
d: Significant for maritime history; its precise aims and outcomes are debated.
Reconfigures the Chola succession through Chalukya-Chola ties and maintains an important phase of political power.
Vikrama Chola, Kulottunga II, Rajaraja II, Rajadhiraja II and Kulottunga III among the rulers before decline in the thirteenth century.
Royal officers, mandalam/valanadu/nadu structures, inscriptions, land revenue and local assemblies; local autonomy had limits and varied by place.
Tanks, canals, reservoirs and maintenance obligations; study inscriptions rather than assuming a uniform model.
Bronze icons, temple sculpture, inscriptions and monumental architecture; religious patronage existed alongside political and economic purposes.
Vishnuvardhana, Ballala II, Narasimha I/II, Vira Ballala III; Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura temple traditions.
Rudrama Devi, Ganapati Deva and Prataparudra II; forts, tanks, temple patronage and regional administration.
Bhillama V, Singhana II and successors; conflict with neighbouring Deccan powers and later Sultanate expansion.
Regional trade, temple institutions and maritime connections develop amid Chola decline.
Competition with Pandyas, Hoysalas and other powers changes the south Indian political map.

t: North-western incursions, Rajput states and the approach to Sultanate rule
d: This group places incursions and regional state histories side by side. “Rajput” identity and clan narratives developed historically and varied across time; genealogies can mix inscriptions, later chronicles and origin traditions.
part: Indian History · PART III — EARLY MEDIEVAL INDIA

d: Muhammad ibn Qasim’s campaign brings parts of Sind under Umayyad control; political and cultural interaction extends unevenly beyond the conquered area.
Chahamanas/Chauhans, Chaulukyas/Solankis, Tomaras, Paramaras, Chandellas, Gahadavalas, Guhilas/Sisodias and Kalachuris; rivalries and alliances are central.
Anangpal traditions are important in later memory; chronology and the historical details of early rulers require caution.

t: Cambrian Period begins; many major animal groups become more visible in the fossil record.
Permian–Triassic mass extinction reshapes life on Earth.
Cretaceous–Palaeogene extinction eliminates non-avian dinosaurs and opens ecological opportunities for mammals.
Early hominins appear in Africa; the evolutionary tree includes multiple branches, not a single straight line.
Stone tools are known from Lomekwi, Kenya; this evidence predates the long-established Oldowan record.
Early Homo appears in the fossil record; Oldowan-style stone-tool traditions become important in the archaeological record.
Oldowan-style stone tools become a well-documented archaeological tradition in East Africa; flakes, cores and choppers support varied cutting and processing tasks.
Homo erectus / related early Homo populations spread beyond Africa into parts of Eurasia; dates and species attribution vary by site.
Acheulean hand-axe and cleaver technologies spread across parts of Africa, western Asia and South Asia.
Acheulean tools and changing hominin dispersals are documented in parts of Africa and Eurasia; stone-tool labels describe technologies, not necessarily a single people or species.
Human populations adapt to changing climates and habitats through varied diets, mobility, cooperative foraging and increasingly complex tools.
Repeated evidence for controlled fire and hearth use becomes clearer at some sites; claims for the earliest fire require site-by-site evaluation.
Complex hunting, shelters and increasingly diverse stone-tool strategies are documented at multiple sites.
Early Homo sapiens fossils appear in Africa; modern human origins are pan-African and evolutionary, not a single sudden event.
Human populations develop varied symbolic practices and long-distance exchange; evidence is uneven and increasingly diverse.
Homo sapiens dispersals beyond Africa occur in multiple episodes; not every early dispersal leads to lasting settlement outside Africa.
Major migrations of Homo sapiens into wider Eurasia take place; interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans leaves genetic evidence in many populations.
People occupy Sahul, the combined Ice Age landmass of Australia and New Guinea; the route and exact timing remain researched.
p: at least c. 50,000 years ago (minimum dates vary)

t: Homo sapiens populations spread through much of Europe; art, ornaments and specialised tools become more visible in many contexts.
People settle many parts of Island Southeast Asia; maritime crossings and changing shorelines make routes and exact dates difficult to reconstruct.
Rock art and portable art traditions appear in multiple regions; the oldest claimed dates are debated and should be tied to the site evidence.
Upper Palaeolithic cultures in many regions use blade technologies, bone tools, ornaments, figurines, music and cave/rock art; traditions differ substantially by region.
Upper Palaeolithic communities develop highly local tool traditions, clothing technologies and resource strategies suited to diverse climates.
Human settlement of the Americas expands; archaeological evidence supports entry and dispersal before 15,000 years ago, with chronology and routes still debated.
Evidence for human presence in the Americas becomes stronger at multiple archaeological sites; dates before this range remain contested at some sites.
Last Glacial Maximum and subsequent warming alter coastlines, migration corridors, vegetation and animal distributions.
Jōmon communities in the Japanese archipelago are associated with some of the world’s earliest pottery traditions; ceramic use predates agriculture in this region.
Late Palaeolithic / Epipalaeolithic communities in several regions develop varied settlement, food collection, fishing, storage and symbolic traditions.
Natufian communities in the Levant show semi-sedentary settlement and intensive use of wild cereals before full farming.
Rock art, ritual places and long-term landscape knowledge continue across multiple continents; no single global “art origin” explains the evidence.
The Pleistocene ends and the Holocene begins; warming conditions support new ecological and settlement patterns.
Early cultivation, animal management and settled life emerge at different rates in Southwest Asia, China, New Guinea, Africa, the Americas and other regions.
Neolithic transitions begin in Southwest Asia and later in other independent centres; farming and herding emerge through different pathways, not a single worldwide invention.
Permanent or long-lived settlements grow in parts of the Levant, including Jericho; settlement history does not by itself mean a state or city civilisation.
Communities combine wild-resource collection, cultivation, ritual activity, storage and long-term building; the transition to farming is gradual.
Cultivation and domestication of wheat, barley, legumes, sheep, goats, pigs and cattle develop across Southwest Asia over generations.
Independent domestication pathways develop, including squash and other crops in the Americas and horticultural systems in New Guinea; exact species dates vary.
p: c. 8000–5000 BCE, Americas and New Guinea (broad ranges)

t: Agriculture and village life develop in parts of China, including millet-based northern systems and rice cultivation in southern/eastern areas.
Early farming and herding practices develop or spread in parts of New Guinea, Africa and other regions; dates and domestication pathways vary.
Mehrgarh in the north-western South Asian region provides evidence of early farming, herding and settled village life.
Çatalhöyük and other Anatolian settlements illustrate dense village life, specialised production and changing ritual practices; their social organisation is debated.
Ceramic traditions, textile production, storage, exchange networks, animal management and specialised crafts become more widespread.
Copper use expands in some regions; Chalcolithic / Copper-Stone communities combine stone tools with early metalworking.
Large settlements, irrigation experiments, craft specialisation and administrative recording develop in several regions, preparing the ground for early urban states.
