t: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia grows into a major urban centre; temples, craft production, cylinder seals and administrative systems expand.
Proto-cuneiform accounting records emerge in southern Mesopotamia; early writing develops from practical administrative needs.
Predynastic Egyptian communities along the Nile form increasingly integrated political and cultural networks.
Early Harappan / regional settlement phases develop in the Indus and neighbouring regions; cultural development is gradual and geographically varied.
Egyptian hieroglyphic writing develops in royal and administrative contexts; the emergence of writing is a process, not a single invention date.
Early city institutions use seals, tokens, accounting marks and written records to manage goods, labour and ritual obligations.
Political unification of Egypt is conventionally associated with Narmer / Menes; royal traditions and modern identification are not identical.
Egypt’s Early Dynastic Period consolidates kingship, writing, administration and royal burial practices.
Norte Chico / Caral in coastal Peru develops monumental centres and complex communities; it is an early independent centre of urban development in the Americas.
Early Dynastic Sumer: city-states such as Ur, Uruk, Lagash and Kish compete and cooperate; kingship, temples, irrigation and scribal learning shape governance.
Egypt’s Old Kingdom: pyramid-building and strong royal institutions; principal rulers include Djoser, Sneferu, Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure.
Djoser and the Step Pyramid at Saqqara mark a major stage in monumental stone architecture; architect Imhotep is traditionally associated with the complex.
Sneferu’s reign is associated with major pyramid experiments, including the Bent Pyramid and Red Pyramid.
Great Pyramid of Khufu and other Giza pyramids are built during Egypt’s Fourth Dynasty.

Mature Harappan / Indus Civilisation: planned cities such as Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi; standardised weights, seals, craft production and wide exchange networks; script remains undeciphered.
The Indus region, Gulf and Mesopotamia exchange goods through maritime and overland contacts; Mesopotamian records mention a place often read as Meluhha, commonly connected with the Indus region.
Nubian / Kerma centres south of Egypt develop their own political institutions, crafts and trade; Nubian history is not merely an appendix to Egyptian history.
Akkadian, Sumerian, Gulf, Iranian, Central Asian and Indus-linked exchange networks connect metals, stones, timber, textiles and agricultural goods across long distances.
Akkadian Empire: Sargon of Akkad and successors establish one of the earliest known territorial empires in Mesopotamia; exact chronology and the empire’s reach vary by reconstruction.
Akkadian, Elamite, Sumerian and other Mesopotamian states interact through war, trade, tribute and court diplomacy.
The First Intermediate Period in Egypt sees competing regional rulers and changing royal authority before reunification under Theban kings.

Climate disruption and political reorganisation affect several regions, including Egypt and parts of West Asia; environmental change is one factor among several, not a universal single cause of collapse.
Ur III / Neo-Sumerian state builds an extensive bureaucratic and taxation system under rulers including Ur-Nammu and Shulgi.
Egypt’s Middle Kingdom and associated intermediate phases: rulers such as Mentuhotep II, Senusret III and Amenemhat III consolidate royal power, administration and frontier networks.
Elamite states in south-western Iran interact with Mesopotamian cities and dynasties; the region has its own political and cultural traditions.
The Indus script, seals, weights and urban craft traditions form a distinctive system; attempts to read the undeciphered script remain unconfirmed.
Old Babylonian and neighbouring Amorite kingdoms rise in Mesopotamia; competing courts, diplomacy, law and literature flourish.
Minoan civilisation develops on Crete, with palace centres, maritime trade, writing systems and distinctive art.
Post-urban / Late Harappan transformations across the Indus region: settlement patterns, trade and material culture change; explanations are multi-causal and vary regionally.
Mycenaean Greek palace societies emerge in the Aegean; Linear B is used for an early form of Greek.
Babylonian and Assyrian centres develop alongside palace societies in Anatolia and the Aegean; diplomatic tablets document cross-regional networks.
Hittite political power grows in Anatolia; later Hittite kings compete with Egypt and other West Asian powers.
Hammurabi rules Babylon; his law collection survives as a major source for kingship, social hierarchy, property and judicial ideals, but should not be read as a complete record of everyday practice.
The Second Intermediate Period in Egypt is marked by competing rulers in the north and south and by Hyksos power in the Delta.
Hyksos rulers govern parts of northern Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period; Egyptian sources reflect later royal perspectives as well as political conflict.

Shang dynasty in China: bronze ritual vessels, oracle-bone inscriptions, royal lineages and warfare; rulers include Wu Ding. Earlier Xia traditions are important in Chinese historiography, but their status as a fully documented dynasty remains debated.
Ahmose I expels Hyksos rulers and begins Egypt’s New Kingdom, a major phase of imperial expansion.
New Kingdom Egypt: Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Amenhotep III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, Seti I and Ramesses II are among the most prominent rulers.
Nubian political power changes over time; later Kushite rulers become major participants in Nile Valley politics.
Vedic traditions develop in South Asia; dates refer to broad linguistic, cultural and textual processes, not to a single dated event.
Kassite Babylon, Mitanni, Assyria, Hittite Anatolia, Mycenaean Greece and New Kingdom Egypt form a diplomatic and commercial Bronze Age world.
Hatshepsut governs Egypt and sponsors trade expeditions and monumental building; her reign challenges simplistic assumptions about ancient political roles and royal power.
Thutmose III expands Egypt’s military and diplomatic influence in the Levant; dates vary by chronology.
Mycenaean palace centres use Linear B records for goods, land and labour; their destruction or transformation is part of the late Bronze Age disruption.
Diplomatic letters, royal marriage, gift exchange, tribute, trade and shared elite culture link courts from Egypt to Mesopotamia and Anatolia.
Akhenaten promotes the worship of the Aten in a dramatic royal religious reform; its scope, motives and social reach remain debated.
Tutankhamun reigns during the restoration of older cults; his tomb’s discovery in 1922 later transforms public knowledge of Egyptian archaeology.
Cities, palace systems and trade networks remain powerful in many regions, while local political and environmental pressures accumulate.
Ramesses II reigns in Egypt, known for monumental construction and the Battle of Kadesh against the Hittites; a later peace treaty is an important diplomatic text.

Late Bronze Age disruption affects parts of the eastern Mediterranean and West Asia: palace systems collapse or transform, migrations and warfare increase, and new polities emerge. Avoid treating this as one simultaneous worldwide “collapse”.
Iron Age, Axial-Age Thought And The Rise Of Classical States
part: World History · PART III — IRON AGE, AXIAL-AGE THOUGHT AND THE RISE OF CLASSICAL STATES

t: Iron use expands in parts of Anatolia, the eastern Mediterranean, South Asia and Africa; adoption is uneven and does not by itself explain social change.
New Iron Age communities form in the Levant and Aegean; Phoenician maritime networks and alphabetic writing help connect Mediterranean shores.
Israelite and Judahite traditions emerge in the southern Levant; biblical narratives, archaeology and later textual traditions must be assessed together and critically.
Western Zhou dynasty in China follows the Shang; the “Mandate of Heaven” becomes an influential political concept in later accounts of legitimate rule.
Zhou forces defeat the Shang; the Zhou dynasty becomes the longest conventionally recognised Chinese dynasty, with later periods of declining central authority.
Neo-Assyrian power grows in northern Mesopotamia, eventually building a large empire through military expansion, provincial government and deportation policies.
Phoenician cities including Tyre, Sidon and Byblos expand Mediterranean trade and settlement networks; Phoenician writing influences later alphabetic systems.
Iron Age cultures, kingdoms and trade networks develop across different parts of Africa, Eurasia and the Americas; no single regional chronology applies everywhere.
Neo-Assyrian Empire: major rulers include Ashurnasirpal II, Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II, Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal; imperial expansion ends after rebellions and attacks by coalition forces.
Olmec centres such as San Lorenzo and La Venta flourish in Mesoamerica; monumental sculpture and long-distance cultural influence are important features.
Greek Archaic period: polis communities, colonisation around the Mediterranean and Black Sea, epic traditions, lyric poetry and new political forms grow.
First recorded Olympic festival in the conventional Greek chronology; sporting and religious traditions predate the surviving written lists.
Western Zhou court loses its capital after attacks and political crisis; the Eastern Zhou period begins.
Spring and Autumn period in China: Zhou kings retain symbolic status while regional lords compete and reform their states.
Traditional foundation date of Rome; archaeology shows a gradual settlement history rather than a single founding moment.
Homeric epics take shape in oral and written traditions; exact authorship and dates are debated.
Assyria conquers the northern Kingdom of Israel; deportation and resettlement reshape the region.
Greek colonisation and trade produce settlements around the Black Sea, Sicily, southern Italy and other Mediterranean shores; local societies shape each encounter.
Etruscan city-states influence early Rome and central Italy; historical traditions about Rome’s kings combine legend and later memory.
Greek and Near Eastern intellectual worlds interact through trade, travel and political contact; early natural philosophy appears in Ionian cities.
Sparta and other Greek poleis develop distinct political and military institutions; later accounts often idealise their systems.
Neo-Babylonian Empire rises under Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II; Babylon becomes a major imperial and monumental centre.
Nineveh falls to a coalition led by Babylonians and Medes, marking the collapse of Assyrian central power.
Zoroastrian traditions develop over a long and debated chronology; Zarathustra’s precise dates remain uncertain.
Laozi is associated with Daoism; the textual history of the *Daodejing* and the historicity of an individual founder are debated.
Mahajanapadas and territorial states develop in South Asia alongside urbanisation, coinage, ironworking and new religious movements.
Lydia in western Anatolia becomes associated with early coinage; coin use spreads through regional trade and state finance.
Vardhamana Mahavira, a key teacher of Jainism, is conventionally dated to this period in older traditions; many modern scholars place his life within a broader sixth–fifth-century BCE range.
Solon’s reforms in Athens address debt, status and political participation; their precise effects and later interpretation are debated.
Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, teaches in northern South Asia; the dates of his life and the early Buddhist chronology remain debated.
p: c. 563–483 BCE (traditional dates; modern estimates vary)

t: Confucius teaches in China; later Confucian traditions profoundly influence ethics, government, education and family ideals across East Asia.
Cyrus II (“the Great”) establishes Persian imperial power by conquering the Medes and building a multiethnic empire.

Achaemenid Persian Empire: rulers include Cyrus II, Cambyses II, Darius I, Xerxes I, Artaxerxes I and Darius III; provincial administration, roads, tribute and royal inscriptions connect a vast territory.
Cyrus captures Babylon; the Persian Empire incorporates Mesopotamia and other major West Asian centres.
Darius I reorganises Achaemenid imperial administration, expands infrastructure and campaigns in regions including the Aegean and Indus frontier.
Cleisthenes’ reforms in Athens are a key stage in the development of Athenian democratic institutions; participation remained restricted by gender, status and citizenship.
Early Buddhist, Jain, Confucian, Daoist, Greek philosophical and Hebrew prophetic traditions are developing or being transmitted; their beginnings should not be compressed into one exact year.
Classical Antiquity And The Great Empires
rel: Long-Run History of the World Economy
part: World History · PART IV — CLASSICAL ANTIQUITY AND THE GREAT EMPIRES

t: Athenian democracy develops through assembly, councils and popular courts, while women, enslaved persons and resident foreigners remain excluded from citizenship.
The Achaemenid administrative system governs diverse peoples through satrapies, tribute, royal roads, multilingual records and local intermediaries.
Classical Athens develops political institutions, drama, philosophy, sculpture and architecture under leaders including Pericles; slavery and exclusion remain central features of the society.
Greco-Persian conflicts, including the Ionian Revolt and Persian Wars, reshape relations between Achaemenid Persia and Greek city-states.
Athenians and allies defeat a Persian force at Marathon; the battle later becomes central to Greek civic memory.
Thermopylae and Salamis mark major episodes in Xerxes I’s invasion of Greece; Greek resistance includes several city-states and naval forces.
Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta and their allies weakens many Greek city-states; causes include rivalry, alliances and competing political systems.
Herodotus and Thucydides write influential histories, developing different approaches to inquiry, evidence, causation and narrative.
Plato and Aristotle shape influential philosophical traditions; Socrates is known chiefly through later accounts by his students and other writers.
Philip II of Macedon consolidates Macedonia and gains dominance in much of Greece.
Alexander the Great conquers the Achaemenid Empire and campaigns through Egypt, Central Asia and north-western South Asia; his empire fragments after his death.
Hellenistic kingdoms emerge: Ptolemaic Egypt, Seleucid territories, Antigonid Macedonia and other successor states; Greek, Egyptian, Persian and local traditions interact.
Mauryan Empire in South Asia: Chandragupta Maurya, Bindusara and Ashoka are the best-known rulers; administrative reach varied and should not be imagined as uniform control over every region.
Seleucus I and Chandragupta Maurya conclude an agreement after conflict; the episode exemplifies diplomatic links across western and South Asian imperial worlds.
Buddhist institutions spread beyond their initial South Asian regions through monastic communities, royal patronage and merchant networks.
The Library and Museum of Alexandria become emblematic of Hellenistic scholarship; scholars work across mathematics, astronomy, medicine and textual criticism.
Ashoka rules the Mauryan Empire; after the Kalinga war he promotes dhamma through inscriptions and supports Buddhist institutions, while imperial policy remains complex.
First Punic War between Rome and Carthage establishes Rome as a major western Mediterranean naval power.
Qin Shi Huang unifies much of China, standardising measures, coinage, script forms and administrative systems; Qin rule is short-lived but profoundly influential.
Qin dynasty centralises government through commanderies, laws, infrastructure and coercive labour; rebellions follow the first emperor’s death.
Second Punic War: Hannibal’s campaign and Rome’s eventual victory shift the Mediterranean balance of power.
Han dynasty governs China, with interruptions by the Xin regime; prominent rulers include Liu Bang / Emperor Gaozu, Emperor Wen, Emperor Jing, Emperor Wu and later Guangwu.
Liu Bang establishes the Han dynasty after the collapse of Qin; the new regime retains centralised structures but adjusts earlier harsh policies.
Roman forces defeat Carthage’s army at Zama; Carthage remains a regional state until Rome destroys the city in 146 BCE.
The Xiongnu confederation becomes a major power on China’s northern frontier; Han and Xiongnu relations combine warfare, diplomacy, trade and marriage alliances.
Silk Roads and maritime routes develop as connected networks rather than a single road; merchants, monks, envoys and migrants carry goods, beliefs and technologies.
Maccabean revolt and the formation of Hasmonean power reshape Jewish political and religious history in Judea.
Parthian Arsacid power expands in Iran and Mesopotamia, competing with Hellenistic states and later Rome.
Rome destroys Carthage and defeats Corinth; Roman power expands across the western Mediterranean.
Emperor Wu of Han expands state power, campaigns against the Xiongnu, supports Confucian state learning and develops frontier and trade links.
Tiberius Gracchus’ land reforms and political crisis mark growing tensions in the Roman Republic.
Marius, Sulla, Pompey, Crassus and Julius Caesar feature in the Roman Republic’s military and political crises.
The Roman Republic’s expansion around the Mediterranean intensifies wealth concentration, land conflict, slavery and struggles over citizenship.
Julius Caesar rises through Roman politics and conquest; civil war and concentration of power undermine Republican norms.
Teotihuacan grows in central Mexico; its later urban scale and influence connect multiple Mesoamerican regions.
Spartacus-led revolt becomes one of the most famous slave uprisings in Roman history.
Caesar’s campaigns in Gaul expand Roman control and his own political and military influence.
Caesar’s civil war ends in his victory over rivals; the Republic’s institutions are severely weakened.
Julius Caesar is assassinated; ensuing civil wars lead toward one-man rule.
Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra; Egypt becomes a Roman province.
Octavian becomes Augustus, conventionally marking the start of the Roman Principate / imperial period.
Pax Romana describes a long phase of relative internal stability in much of the Roman Empire, although frontiers, rebellions and wars continued.
The Kushan and other Central Asian polities help connect caravan routes between South Asia, Central Asia and western China.
The Roman imperial economy uses roads, ports, coinage, taxation, slave labour and regional specialisation; prosperity and coercion coexist.
Christian movements emerge from Jewish contexts in the Roman eastern Mediterranean; dates for Jesus’ life and early Christian texts are approximate and debated.
Roman defeat in the Teutoburg Forest prevents permanent Roman annexation of much of Germania east of the Rhine.
Fire in Rome during Nero’s reign leads to major rebuilding; later Christian accounts link the episode to persecution, but the evidence requires care.
Roman forces destroy the Second Temple in Jerusalem after revolt; the event profoundly reshapes Jewish religious history.
Mount Vesuvius erupts, burying Pompeii and Herculaneum; archaeological remains preserve unusual evidence of Roman urban life.
The period of the so-called Five Good Emperors and their successors includes Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius and Commodus; the label is a later historical judgement.
Trajan expands Roman territory to its greatest extent by area; later emperors consolidate rather than sustain every eastern conquest.
Aksum emerges as a major state in the Horn of Africa, using Red Sea commerce and coinage to connect Africa, Arabia and the Mediterranean.
Kushan power links parts of Central Asia and South Asia; Kanishka is a prominent ruler, but his accession date and some chronological details are disputed.
Cai Lun is credited in Chinese tradition with improving papermaking; earlier paper-like materials existed, and technological development was cumulative.
p: c. 105 CE (traditional date of court report)

t: Trajan’s campaigns reach the Persian Gulf, marking one of the broadest eastern expansions of the Roman Empire.
Hadrian emphasises consolidation, provincial administration and frontier works, including major projects in Britain.
Roman trade with the Indian Ocean world and East Asia forms part of an expanding Afro-Eurasian commercial system.
Marcus Aurelius rules amid wars and plague; his *Meditations* later becomes an influential work of Stoic philosophy.
Maya cities grow in Mesoamerica, with writing, calendrical knowledge, monumental architecture and dynastic inscriptions.

part: World History · PART V — LATE ANTIQUITY AND CLASSICAL TRANSFORMATIONS

t: The Yellow Turban Rebellion begins in Han China in 184 CE; it intensifies strains on imperial authority.
Gupta power emerges in northern India; dates for early rulers and the dynasty’s origins are not fully certain.
Han dynasty ends; Three Kingdoms and later reunification struggles reshape China.
Third-Century Crisis in the Roman Empire: civil wars, rapid imperial turnover, invasions and economic pressures.
Classic Maya period, with powerful city-states, royal inscriptions, calendrics, monumental architecture and complex inter-city conflict; dates differ by city.
Moche, Nazca, Tiwanaku and Wari societies develop across the Andes and adjacent regions; their chronologies and political structures vary.
Christian communities expand in some Roman cities while facing periodic persecution; experiences differ by emperor, region and community.
The capture of Emperor Valerian by the Sasanians reveals the vulnerability of Roman eastern frontiers during the third-century crisis.
Diocletian reforms Roman administration and taxation and establishes a tetrarchic system to govern the empire.
Gupta Empire reaches a major phase of power and cultural production; principal rulers include Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta.
King Ezana of Aksum is associated with the adoption of Christianity by the royal court; Aksum’s Red Sea position supports long-distance trade.
Constantine I becomes emperor, supports Christianity and founds Constantinople as an imperial capital in 330 CE.
Edict of Milan, traditionally associated with Constantine and Licinius, grants toleration to Christians within the Roman Empire.
Vakataka power in the Deccan overlaps with Gupta politics and supports art, religious patronage and regional statecraft.
Council of Nicaea addresses Christian doctrinal disputes; later church councils continue to shape Christian orthodoxy.
Constantinople is formally inaugurated as an imperial capital, becoming a major political, commercial and religious centre.
Hunnic and other migrations, wars and political changes reshape Eurasia; explanations involve diverse groups rather than one simple invasion.
Battle of Adrianople exposes vulnerabilities in Roman frontier and military systems.
Theodosius I’s government gives Nicene Christianity a privileged position in the Roman Empire.
After Theodosius I, Roman imperial administration is conventionally described as divided between eastern and western courts; the empire remains linked in law and political ideology.
Bantu-language-speaking communities continue dispersals and local state formation across large parts of sub-equatorial Africa; timing and pathways vary by region.
Classical Sanskrit literature, drama, mathematics, astronomy and religious scholarship develop through multiple courts and institutions; cultural achievements cannot be assigned to one dynasty alone.
Visigoths sack Rome under Alaric; the symbolic event becomes a major reference point in later narratives of Rome’s transformation.
Southern and Northern dynasties govern divided China; Buddhism and new forms of court culture spread and evolve.
Vandals establish control over North Africa, including Carthage, disrupting Roman Mediterranean power.
Battle of the Catalaunian Plains involves Roman and allied forces against Attila’s Huns; later accounts exaggerate or simplify the battle’s decisiveness.
Vandals sack Rome; western imperial authority continues to weaken.
Odoacer deposes the last western Roman emperor, Romulus Augustulus; the eastern Roman / Byzantine Empire continues for nearly a millennium.
Clovis I expands Frankish power in Gaul and adopts Nicene Christianity; later Frankish kingdoms shape western European politics.
The Sasanian Empire in Iran and the Eastern Roman / Byzantine Empire remain rival great powers; rulers such as Kavad I and later Khosrow I reform administration and military structures.
Korean kingdoms develop writing, Buddhist institutions and relations with China and Japan; cultural transmission is reciprocal and locally adapted.
Japan’s Yamato court develops central authority and exchanges with the Korean peninsula and China; many details of early court chronology are reconstructed from later chronicles.
Justinian I rules the Byzantine Empire, commissions a major legal compilation, sponsors Hagia Sophia and attempts reconquest in parts of the former western empire.
The Silk Road, Indian Ocean routes and Red Sea trade continue to transmit goods, religious traditions, artistic forms and diseases across connected regions.
Nika Riots in Constantinople expose urban and political tensions during Justinian’s reign; the revolt is suppressed and major rebuilding follows.
The Plague of Justinian affects the Mediterranean and adjoining regions; estimates of mortality and the demographic consequences remain debated.
Silk production and other technologies move between states through migration, espionage, craft exchange and trade; individual “invention stories” often compress a longer process.
The Gupta imperial structure has fragmented; numerous regional states succeed it, while Sanskritic learning and religious institutions continue to develop.
Birth of Muhammad is conventionally placed around 570 CE in Islamic tradition.
The Sasanian-Byzantine rivalry intensifies; the later war of 602–628 exhausts both empires before the early Islamic conquests.
Early Post-Classical Worlds And Expanding Networks
part: World History · PART VI — EARLY POST-CLASSICAL WORLDS AND EXPANDING NETWORKS

t: Sui dynasty briefly reunifies China and restores large-scale state projects; heavy burdens and rebellions contribute to its fall.
Muhammad is said to receive the first revelations; Islamic tradition dates the beginning of his prophetic mission to this period.

Tang dynasty in China: prominent rulers include Taizong, Gaozong, Empress Wu Zetian and Xuanzong; cosmopolitan cities, poetry, Buddhism, trade and state examinations flourish, alongside rebellions and fiscal strain.
Hijra: Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina; the event marks the starting point of the Islamic calendar.
Muhammad’s return to Mecca in the Islamic traditional chronology marks a decisive shift in the peninsula’s political and religious landscape.
Muhammad dies; leadership of the Muslim community passes to the caliphs, producing debates and divisions over authority.
Rashidun Caliphate: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali; rapid expansion into parts of Byzantine and Sasanian territory, alongside internal civil conflict.
Arab-Muslim conquests take major Byzantine and Sasanian territories; the Sasanian Empire ends, while Byzantine rule survives in reduced form.
Umayyad Caliphate, centred first at Damascus; rulers include Muawiya I, Abd al-Malik and al-Walid I; Arabic administration and coinage expand across a vast empire.
Srivijaya grows as a maritime power centred on Sumatra, connecting the Strait of Malacca, Buddhist learning and Indian Ocean trade.
The Battle of Karbala and the death of Husayn ibn Ali become central to Shi’a religious memory and the historical development of Sunni–Shi’a distinctions.
Empress Wu Zetian rules in China in her own name after rising through court politics; her reign complicates later assumptions about female political authority.
Nara becomes Japan’s capital; the Nara period sees the consolidation of court institutions, Buddhist patronage and written chronicles.
Umayyad forces cross into Iberia; Muslim-ruled al-Andalus develops over subsequent centuries amid changing Christian and Muslim polities.
The Abbasid movement challenges Umayyad rule; the transition to a new caliphate is accompanied by regional political change.
Abbasid Revolution ends Umayyad rule in most of the central Islamic lands; a surviving Umayyad branch establishes power in al-Andalus.
The Abbasid world supports translation, medicine, mathematics, astronomy, philosophy and literature; “Islamic Golden Age” is a broad label for diverse and uneven developments.
Battle of Talas pits Abbasid-allied forces against Tang China; later accounts overstate its role in the spread of papermaking, which moved through a more complex history.
Abbasid caliph al-Mansur establishes Baghdad as a new capital, which becomes a major centre of scholarship, trade and imperial administration.
Al-Khwarizmi and other scholars contribute to mathematics and astronomy; the word “algorithm” derives from the Latinised form of al-Khwarizmi’s name.
Raid on Lindisfarne is a conventional marker for Viking attacks on England; Scandinavian activity also includes trade, settlement, craft and state formation.
Heian-kyo (Kyoto) becomes Japan’s capital; court culture, literature and Buddhist institutions develop.
Ghana / Wagadou becomes a major West African power linked to gold, salt and trans-Saharan exchange; its chronology is reconstructed from archaeology and later written accounts.
Charlemagne is crowned emperor in Rome; Carolingian political and educational renewal affects much of western and central Europe.
Viking maritime activity expands across the North Atlantic, British Isles, continental Europe and river routes to eastern Europe.
Classic Maya cities decline or transform in parts of the southern lowlands; many Maya communities and political traditions continue elsewhere.
Kievan Rus’ emerges along river and trade routes connecting the Baltic, Black Sea and Byzantine worlds; origins and early rulers are debated in scholarship.
Jayavarman II is associated with the emergence of Angkorian kingship in Cambodia; later rulers build a powerful agrarian and temple-centred state.
Chola power rises in southern India and becomes an important Indian Ocean participant; its strongest phase overlaps with many Southeast Asian states.
The Diamond Sutra, a dated printed Buddhist text from Dunhuang, is a landmark in the surviving history of printing.
Korean Silla loses central control; later states and the Goryeo dynasty reshape the peninsula.
Household, court and scholarly cultures across the Abbasid world draw on Arabic, Persian, Greek, Syriac and other languages and traditions.
Paper-making spreads westward from East Asia through complex transfers across Central and West Asia; local workshops adapt materials and methods.
Trans-Saharan exchange links salt, gold, textiles, books and people; camel transport helps make regular desert crossings more viable.
The Swahili coast develops distinctive urban cultures from African foundations, with Arabic, Persian, Indian and later Chinese connections.
The Khmer, Cham, Javanese and Malay worlds develop temple centres, ports, agrarian systems and maritime networks.
Tang dynasty ends after rebellions and fragmentation; the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period precedes Song reunification.
Song dynasty reunifies much of China; commercial growth, printing, urban life, science and examination bureaucracy develop, though northern frontier pressures persist.
Fatimid power expands in North Africa; the Fatimid Caliphate becomes a major rival to Abbasid and regional authorities.
Norse settlements develop in Iceland and Greenland; contact across the North Atlantic precedes later European voyages to the Americas.
High Medieval Worlds, Empire And Interregional Exchange
rel: Major Economic Powers and Regional Economic Models
Long-Run History of the World Economy
part: World History · PART VII — HIGH MEDIEVAL WORLDS, EMPIRE AND INTERREGIONAL EXCHANGE

t: Song China is a centre of commercial growth, advanced printing, iron production, paper money experiments and maritime trade.
Seljuk Turks rise in Central and West Asia; Seljuk rulers become influential in the Abbasid political world and Anatolia.
Universities and cathedral schools develop in parts of Europe; scholarly work also continues in Islamic, Jewish, Byzantine, South Asian and East Asian settings.
Cahokia in the Mississippi valley becomes one of the largest urban and ceremonial centres in pre-Columbian North America.
The conventional date for the East-West Schism marks a gradual and complex separation between Latin western and Greek eastern Christian churches.
Norman conquest of England under William I links English and continental political cultures and reshapes landholding and governance.
Battle of Manzikert contributes to a transformation of Byzantine authority in Anatolia, although the region’s Turkification occurs over centuries.
Pope Urban II calls for an expedition that becomes the First Crusade; Crusading movements and responses span several centuries and regions.
First Crusade captures Jerusalem in 1099; the Crusader states endure with shifting borders and local alliances.
Angkor and Khmer state systems reach major phases of urban and hydraulic development; rulers include Suryavarman II and Jayavarman VII.
Great Zimbabwe grows as a stone-built political and commercial centre linked to gold and Indian Ocean exchange; local African agency is central to its history.
Swahili city-states along the East African coast connect African hinterlands with Arabia, Persia, India and wider Indian Ocean commerce.
Jurchen Jin dynasty controls much of northern China before Mongol conquest; Song China survives in the south during the Southern Song period.
The Jingkang Incident and loss of northern China lead to the Southern Song court; Chinese political geography changes for more than a century.
Genghis Khan unites Mongol groups and launches conquests that transform Eurasian power relations.
Commercial towns, guilds, merchant law and fairs expand in parts of Europe and across Afro-Eurasian routes.
Islamic scholarship and law develop through madrasas, mosques, courts, libraries and scholarly travel; institutions vary by region.
Goryeo Korea develops celadon, Buddhist printing and court institutions, while negotiating pressures from regional rivals.
Crusaders sack Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade; the Latin Empire briefly occupies the Byzantine capital, deepening eastern Mediterranean divisions.
Temüjin is proclaimed Genghis Khan; the Mongol Empire expands through campaigns, diplomacy and incorporation of conquered populations.
Delhi Sultanate begins under Qutb al-Din Aibak after the Ghurid conquests; the subcontinent remains home to many parallel and regional powers.
Mongol imperial formations under Genghis Khan, Ögedei, Möngke, Kublai and other Chinggisid lineages connect large parts of Eurasia, but successor khanates pursue separate interests.
Albigensian Crusade targets Cathar communities in southern France and strengthens Capetian royal power in the region.
Magna Carta is sealed by King John of England after baronial conflict; its later constitutional significance greatly exceeds its immediate medieval context.
Mongol campaigns devastate Khwarazmian territories and alter the political order of Central Asia and Iran.
Mongol campaigns affect the Caucasus, Rus’ principalities, Central Asia, Iran and other regions; conquest produces destruction as well as new imperial connections.
Mali consolidates control over parts of the Niger region and trans-Saharan trade; rulers after Sunjata expand or reshape the empire.
Sunjata Keita is associated with the foundation of the Mali Empire in West Africa; oral epics, archaeology and written sources each preserve different dimensions of its history.
Mongol armies invade parts of Central Europe; the withdrawal of forces follows political developments within the Mongol Empire, not a single European battlefield defeat.
Mamluk power takes root in Egypt after the Ayyubid period; Mamluk rulers later repel Mongol forces at Ayn Jalut and hold major trade routes.
Mongol forces under Hülegü sack Baghdad, ending Abbasid caliphal rule there and profoundly disrupting the city’s political and scholarly institutions.
Yuan dynasty under the Mongols governs China; Kublai Khan is the best-known ruler. Yuan power combines steppe imperial traditions with Chinese state institutions.
Mongol-led Yuan invasions of Japan fail; storms later called kamikaze in Japanese memory become part of accounts of the campaigns.
The Mamluks capture Acre, conventionally marking the end of major Crusader territorial rule on the mainland Levant.
Majapahit is founded in Java; it becomes an influential Southeast Asian state whose maritime reach is described differently by later sources and modern scholars.
Osman I’s principality is conventionally treated as the origin of the Ottoman dynasty; the early chronology is debated.
Renaissance culture develops in parts of Italy; it overlaps with vigorous intellectual and artistic traditions elsewhere and is not a universal European “rebirth”.
Mali, Songhai precursors, Kanem-Bornu and Hausa trading cities participate in West and Central African political and commercial networks.
Ottoman expansion into the Balkans and Anatolia accelerates under rulers including Murad I and Bayezid I; defeats and recoveries reshape the state.
Mansa Musa rules Mali; his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 becomes famous for its scale and for showing Mali’s connections to wider Islamic and commercial networks.
Tenochtitlan is founded by the Mexica; it later becomes the centre of the Aztec / Triple Alliance power.
Vijayanagara is founded in southern India; its empire becomes a major regional power connected to Indian Ocean and inland trade.
Hundred Years’ War between the English and French crowns involves changing alliances, dynastic claims, taxation, infantry tactics and civilian hardship.
Timur (Tamerlane) rises in Central Asia and creates a large but short-lived conquest empire; his campaigns cause widespread destruction and displacement.
The Black Death spreads across Afro-Eurasia, causing severe mortality and demographic, economic, religious and political change; estimates vary widely by region.
Ming dynasty begins in China after the fall of Yuan rule; Hongwu is the founding emperor.
Ming rulers consolidate state institutions; Yongle later moves the capital to Beijing and sponsors major maritime expeditions.
Inca roads, relay systems, storehouses and labour obligations help connect highland and coastal ecological zones across the Andes.
Inca state expands in the Andes, particularly under Pachacuti; a larger imperial system is built through conquest, labour organisation, roads and regional alliances.
Aztec power expands in central Mexico under the Triple Alliance; tribute networks, warfare, markets and ritual shape imperial organisation.
The Ethiopian Zagwe dynasty and later Solomonic rulers support Christian institutions and architecture; regional relations include trade, war and diplomacy.
Admiral Zheng He leads Ming maritime expeditions across the Indian Ocean, reaching ports in Southeast Asia, South Asia, Arabia and East Africa.
Pachacuti and successors, including Topa Inca Yupanqui, expand the Inca polity into a major Andean empire.
Ottoman power expands in Anatolia and the Balkans; regional states adapt to changing military technologies and diplomatic alignments.
The spread of moveable-type printing in Europe, associated with Johannes Gutenberg, accelerates text reproduction; printing technologies already have long histories in East Asia.

part: World History · PART VIII — EARLY MODERN GLOBAL CONNECTIONS

t: European Renaissance art, scholarship and humanism flourish in different centres; developments draw on ancient texts, local traditions and knowledge transmitted through Islamic and other scholarly networks.
Portuguese voyaging along West African coasts develops in the setting of older African trade and political systems; overseas expansion is inseparable from coercion and slavery.
Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captures Constantinople; the Byzantine imperial state ends, while the city becomes an Ottoman capital and remains a major global centre.
Bartolomeu Dias rounds the southern tip of Africa, demonstrating a viable sea route between the Atlantic and Indian Ocean systems.
Columbus reaches the Caribbean under the Spanish crown; this begins sustained transatlantic contact, conquest, colonisation and the Columbian Exchange, not the first human presence in the Americas.
Treaty of Tordesillas divides claimed overseas spheres between Portugal and Spain; Indigenous peoples and other powers are excluded from the agreement.
Vasco da Gama reaches the Indian Ocean coast of South Asia by sailing around Africa; maritime commerce and armed imperial competition intensify.
The Portuguese establish fortified trading networks in the Indian Ocean; existing Muslim, African, Gujarati, Arab, Persian and Southeast Asian commercial networks remain indispensable.

The Atlantic slave trade expands under European empires; African societies, merchants, states and captives experience varied and often devastating effects, and forced labour becomes central to plantation economies.
Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal and European dynastic states expand or consolidate with gunpowder armies, fiscal institutions and negotiated elite alliances.
Safavid dynasty is established in Iran under Shah Ismail I; Twelver Shiism becomes a defining feature of the state.
Martin Luther’s challenge to indulgence practices becomes a conventional starting marker for the Protestant Reformation; wider reform movements have multiple causes and precedents.
Protestant reform spreads through print, preaching, universities and urban networks; Lutheran, Reformed, Anabaptist and other traditions diverge.
Hernán Cortés reaches the Mexica sphere; Indigenous alliances and political rivalries are crucial to the subsequent conquest.
Hernán Cortés and Indigenous allies overthrow the Mexica-led Aztec Empire; epidemics, alliances, siege warfare and Spanish violence all shape the conquest.
Magellan-Elcano expedition completes the first recorded circumnavigation by a single expedition; Magellan himself dies in the Philippines.
Suleiman I rules the Ottoman Empire at a major height of territorial, legal, architectural and cultural influence.
Babur defeats the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat and establishes Mughal rule in northern India; the early Mughal state still has to secure its power.
Spanish conquest dismantles the Inca imperial state, while resistance and successor communities continue long after the fall of Cusco.
Copernicus publishes a major heliocentric account; European astronomical debates form one strand of the wider history of science.
Council of Trent responds to Protestant challenges and reforms Catholic institutions; the Reformation era reshapes European politics, education and confessional identities.
Catholic reform and the Council of Trent address clergy, doctrine and institutional discipline; Catholic missions later expand globally.
The Safavid and Ottoman empires compete over frontier regions and trade corridors; religious identity and state rivalry interact but do not fully determine policy.
Akbar rules the Mughal Empire, strengthening administration, elite incorporation and imperial culture; policies and their reach changed over the reign.
Battle of Lepanto checks Ottoman naval expansion in the western Mediterranean but does not end Ottoman maritime power.
Tokugawa Ieyasu emerges as a leading Japanese powerbroker amid civil conflict; unification is consolidated in the early seventeenth century.
Gregorian calendar reform is introduced under Pope Gregory XIII; adoption occurs at different times in different states and communities.
Shah Abbas I strengthens Safavid Iran, reforms military structures, develops Isfahan and encourages trade and diplomatic contacts.
English forces defeat the Spanish Armada’s invasion attempt; the wider Anglo-Spanish conflict continues after the Armada’s failure.
Spanish colonial administration develops in the Americas; Indigenous labour, tribute, missionisation and demographic collapse from epidemic disease reshape societies.
Moroccan invasion defeats Songhai forces at Tondibi, contributing to the fragmentation of the Songhai Empire.
English East India Company receives a royal charter; the company later evolves from a trading corporation into a territorial power.
The transatlantic slave trade expands dramatically; African captives are forcibly transported to the Americas, where plantation regimes reshape economies and societies.
Dutch, English and French colonial settlements expand in the Caribbean and North America; Indigenous dispossession and competition among empires intensify.
Dutch East India Company (VOC) is founded and becomes a major armed commercial corporation in Asian and global trade.
Tokugawa shogunate is established under Tokugawa Ieyasu; political order is reorganised through domains, status hierarchies and controlled foreign relations.
Jahangir rules the Mughal Empire; court painting, diplomacy and elite politics flourish amid continuing regional conflicts.
Jamestown becomes the first permanent English settlement in what becomes the United States; Indigenous societies and earlier European settlements form the wider context.
Thirty Years’ War devastates parts of Central Europe and ends with the Peace of Westphalia; religion, dynastic rivalry and state interests intertwine.
Shah Jahan rules the Mughal Empire; court architecture, including the Taj Mahal, becomes emblematic of imperial patronage and labour organisation.
English Civil Wars lead to the execution of Charles I and a republican / Protectorate phase under Oliver Cromwell; the monarchy is restored in 1660.
Qing conquest of Beijing establishes Manchu rule at China’s imperial centre; Qing expansion and consolidation continue over decades.
Scientific Revolution: figures such as Galileo, Kepler, Boyle, Descartes and Newton reshape astronomy, physics, mathematics and natural philosophy.
Kangxi rules the Qing Empire, overseeing consolidation, court scholarship and territorial expansion.
Isaac Newton publishes *Principia Mathematica*, a landmark in classical mechanics and mathematical physics.
Glorious Revolution and English Bill of Rights reshape the English monarchy and parliament; later constitutional interpretations build on these events.
Atlantic plantation economies, global commodity chains, forced migration and intercontinental exchange have become central features of the world economy.

Enlightenment thinkers including Locke, Montesquieu, Voltaire, Hume and others debate reason, rights, government, religion and knowledge; these ideas circulate unevenly and coexist with empire and slavery.
War of the Spanish Succession reshapes European dynastic balance and imperial claims overseas.
Atlantic revolutions are foreshadowed by debates about sovereignty, representation, religious authority, property, enslavement and natural rights.
Act of Union creates the Kingdom of Great Britain by joining England and Scotland; Irish and imperial histories remain distinct parts of the wider British state.
Peter I adopts the title emperor and the Russian Empire becomes a formal imperial state in the early eighteenth century.

t: Industrial Revolution begins in Britain and spreads unevenly; textiles, coal, steam power, iron, factories, railways and later electricity transform production, cities and labour.
Seven Years’ War becomes a global conflict involving Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa and South Asia; Britain and France compete for imperial influence.
Industrialisation expands in Britain; James Watt’s steam-engine improvements are important within a longer history of engineering and energy use.
British colonial rule in Bengal expands after revenue rights are obtained; colonial extraction and Company governance become central to South Asian and global imperial history.
The first industrial changes spread through cotton textiles, coal, iron, steam, canals and factory labour; family economies and urban environments are transformed.
American Revolutionary War leads to independence of the thirteen British colonies; Indigenous nations, enslaved people and other groups experience the conflict differently.
Declaration of Independence issued by the thirteen colonies; its language of equality coexists with slavery, exclusion and dispossession.
US Constitution drafted and ratified; the federal republic develops through later amendments, political conflict and expansion.
French Revolution begins; monarchy, citizenship, class, religion and political authority are contested across Europe and beyond.
Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen articulates principles of rights and citizenship, while women, enslaved people and colonised populations challenge exclusions.
The Haitian Revolution begins in Saint-Domingue; enslaved people, free people of colour and competing European powers pursue conflicting political aims.
Haitian Revolution, led at different stages by figures including Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines, defeats slavery and French colonial rule; Haiti declares independence in 1804.
French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars transform state borders, law, military organisation and political ideologies across Europe and adjacent regions.
Napoleon Bonaparte rises to power, becomes emperor and reshapes much of continental Europe before defeat and exile.
Napoleonic Code is promulgated; it influences civil-law systems, but also embeds patriarchal authority and restrictions.
Britain and other states enact abolition of the slave trade and slavery over time; legal abolition does not immediately end coercive labour or racial hierarchy.
Peninsular War resists Napoleonic rule in Spain and Portugal; it influences political crises and independence movements in Spanish America.
Independence movements across Spanish America produce new republics; leaders include Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín and regional revolutionaries.
Congress of Vienna and post-Napoleonic settlements redraw political arrangements and promote a balance-of-power system.
The Congress System and conservative restoration attempt to maintain a European balance of power after the Napoleonic Wars; liberal and nationalist opposition persists.
Liberalism, nationalism, socialism and constitutionalism expand as political movements; their meanings differ across classes and countries.
Mexico achieves independence from Spain after a long conflict; independence across Latin America proceeds through varied paths.
July Revolution in France changes the monarchy; the same year’s revolutions in Belgium and Poland form part of a wider era of national and constitutional struggles.
Railway networks expand in Britain and elsewhere, changing mobility, markets, military logistics and the scale of state administration.
First Opium War between Qing China and Britain ends with the Treaty of Nanjing, opening treaty ports and imposing unequal arrangements.
Revolutions across Europe challenge monarchies and social hierarchies; nationalist and liberal movements have mixed outcomes.
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels publish *The Communist Manifesto*, a landmark in socialist and communist political thought.
Taiping Rebellion in China becomes one of the deadliest civil conflicts in history; causes include religious visions, social crisis and Qing state weakness.
Crimean War pits Russia against an alliance including the Ottoman Empire, Britain, France and Sardinia; it exposes military and logistical weaknesses.
Second Opium War deepens foreign intervention in Qing China and expands treaty-port concessions.
Charles Darwin publishes *On the Origin of Species*, transforming debates about biological evolution and natural selection.
The Second Industrial Revolution develops through steel, chemicals, electrical systems and new transport and communication technologies.
US Civil War ends slavery in the United States through constitutional change, but racial inequality and political struggle continue.
Italian unification proceeds through wars, diplomacy and popular movements; Rome joins the Kingdom of Italy in 1870.
Meiji Restoration ends Tokugawa shogunal rule and launches state-led modernisation and imperial expansion in Japan.
German unification follows Prussian-led wars; the German Empire becomes a major European power.
European powers impose colonial rule across much of Africa; African resistance, diplomacy, adaptation and state-building continue across regions.
Queen Victoria is proclaimed Empress of India; the British Empire’s global structure continues to change through colonial rule and resistance.
Britain occupies Egypt amid financial and strategic disputes; formal and informal empire overlap in the control of routes and resources.
Berlin Conference formalises rules for European claims in Africa; African states and societies are excluded from the decisions, and colonisation intensifies.
Indian National Congress is founded, part of a wider era of anti-colonial organisation and constitutional politics in Asia and Africa.
The Second International is founded, linking many socialist and labour parties across borders.
Women’s suffrage campaigns grow in Europe, the Americas, Australasia and elsewhere; legal victories occur at different times and often exclude colonised women.
First Sino-Japanese War ends with Japanese victory and reveals the crisis of Qing power and Japan’s rising regional influence.
Ethiopian forces defeat Italy at Adwa; Ethiopia preserves sovereignty in the face of European imperial expansion.
Spanish-American War leads to a major shift in US overseas power and the transfer of Spanish colonial territories.
Second Boer War exposes tensions within the British Empire in southern Africa.
Russo-Japanese War ends with Japan’s victory, reshaping Asian and global perceptions of imperial power.
Russian Revolution of 1905 forces limited political concessions but does not end autocracy.
Young Turk Revolution restores the Ottoman constitution and opens a period of political transformation.
Mexican Revolution challenges the Porfirian order and produces major conflicts over land, labour, constitutional authority and social reform.
Xinhai Revolution ends Qing imperial rule; the Republic of China is proclaimed in 1912.
Balkan Wars reshape southeastern Europe and intensify regional tensions before the First World War.

t: Archduke Franz Ferdinand is assassinated in Sarajevo; the crisis triggers a chain of diplomatic and military decisions leading to world war.
European empires mobilise soldiers and labourers from colonies; the war’s fronts and consequences are global, not only European.
First World War: fighting across Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Asia and the seas; industrial weaponry, mass mobilisation, colonial troops and civilian suffering shape the conflict.
Germany invades Belgium and northern France; the Western Front develops into trench warfare.
Ottoman authorities deport and kill Armenians and other Christian populations; the Armenian genocide is widely recognised by many scholars and states, while denial remains politically contested.
Battles of Verdun and the Somme exemplify the destructive scale of industrial warfare.
Russian Revolutions overthrow the monarchy and bring Bolshevik power; war, land, labour and political crisis are intertwined.
The United States enters the First World War; its economic and military role affects the conflict’s later course.

Balfour Declaration expresses British support for a Jewish national home in Palestine, with language about rights of existing non-Jewish communities; later interpretation and implementation are deeply contested.
Armistice ends major fighting on the Western Front; peace settlements and civil conflicts continue.
Influenza pandemic spreads globally; mortality estimates vary, and wartime movement contributes to rapid transmission.
Treaty of Versailles imposes terms on Germany; other treaties dismantle or reorganise former empires and produce new states.
League of Nations is created as an attempt at collective security; limitations in membership, enforcement and great-power participation weaken it.
The postwar peace settlement creates mandates and new states in former Ottoman and German territories; disputes over borders and self-determination continue.
The May Fourth Movement and other political currents in China challenge imperialism, traditional institutions and the existing political order.
Turkish War of Independence leads to the abolition of the Ottoman sultanate and establishment of the Republic of Turkey under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1923.
League of Nations begins operations; its mandates, minority protections and collective-security systems face major limits.
Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) is established; its political system and planned economy influence global politics for decades.
Fascist regime under Benito Mussolini develops in Italy; authoritarian nationalism becomes a major force in interwar Europe.
Wall Street crash becomes a marker for the Great Depression; banking crisis, unemployment and international economic contraction spread over the following years.
Authoritarian and fascist movements grow amid economic crisis, fear of revolution, nationalism and the erosion of democratic institutions.
Japan occupies Manchuria and establishes Manchukuo; the League of Nations’ response exposes the weakness of collective security.
Adolf Hitler becomes German chancellor; Nazi dictatorship dismantles democratic institutions, persecutes opponents and escalates antisemitic state policy.
Italy invades and occupies Ethiopia, a major example of aggressive fascist imperialism.
Spanish Civil War pits the Republic against Franco’s Nationalists and draws international volunteers and foreign intervention.
Japan launches a full-scale war against China; atrocities include the Nanjing Massacre and wider civilian suffering.
Anschluss incorporates Austria into Nazi Germany; the Munich Agreement cedes the Sudetenland, failing to prevent further aggression.
Germany invades Poland; Britain and France declare war, conventionally marking the start of the Second World War in Europe.
Second World War becomes a global conflict involving Europe, Asia, Africa, the Atlantic and Pacific; mass mobilisation, occupation, genocide and strategic bombing transform societies.
War expands into North Africa and the Mediterranean; colonial troops and imperial resources form a major part of the conflict.
Fall of France and the Battle of Britain mark a critical phase of the European war.
Germany invades the Soviet Union (Operation Barbarossa), opening an enormous eastern front.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor; the United States enters the war against Japan and subsequently Germany and Italy.
The Holocaust: Nazi Germany and collaborators systematically murder six million Jews and persecute and kill Roma, disabled people, Slavs, political opponents, LGBTQ people and others.
War in the Pacific includes Japanese occupation, resistance movements, forced labour, mass civilian deaths and battles across island and mainland Asia.
Battles of Midway, El Alamein and Stalingrad become major turning points in different theatres of the war.
Allied landings in Normandy (D-Day) open a major western front in Nazi-occupied Europe.
Allied and Soviet forces advance into Germany; occupation and the collapse of the Nazi state follow.
The United States drops atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; the human consequences and ethical legacy remain central to nuclear history.
Japan formally surrenders, ending the Second World War; civil wars, decolonisation struggles and occupation transitions continue in several regions.
United Nations is established after the San Francisco Conference; the Charter enters into force on 24 October 1945.

t: Bretton Woods institutions establish frameworks for international monetary cooperation and reconstruction, including the IMF and World Bank.
Nuremberg trials prosecute leading Nazi officials for major international crimes and shape later international criminal law.
Indonesia’s independence struggle confronts Dutch attempts to re-establish colonial rule; international pressure contributes to transfer of sovereignty in 1949.
Decolonisation accelerates in Asia; Indonesia, Vietnam and other societies wage struggles against returning or continuing European colonial power.
Truman Doctrine signals US support for governments resisting communist expansion; containment becomes a central Cold War strategy.
Marshall Plan supports European recovery; rebuilding and political alignment take place amid the emerging division of Europe.
Universal Declaration of Human Rights is adopted by the UN General Assembly; it becomes a landmark statement of international rights principles.
First Arab-Israeli War follows the end of the British Mandate and Israel’s declaration of independence; displacement of Palestinians and the unresolved conflict become enduring regional issues.
North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is founded; security blocs become central to Cold War Europe.
Mao Zedong proclaims the People’s Republic of China after the Chinese Civil War; the Republic of China government retreats to Taiwan.
Federal Republic of Germany and German Democratic Republic are formed in separate political blocs.
Anti-colonial independence movements reshape Asia and Africa; political systems, borders and economic structures differ widely across newly independent states.
Korean War ends in an armistice rather than a peace treaty; the peninsula remains divided.
Egyptian Free Officers overthrow the monarchy; Gamal Abdel Nasser later becomes a leading voice in Arab nationalism and non-alignment.
Algerian War of Independence culminates in the end of French colonial rule; conflict includes guerrilla warfare, repression, settler politics and civilian violence.
Bandung Conference brings Asian and African leaders together; it is a precursor to wider non-aligned and postcolonial diplomacy.
Warsaw Pact formalises the Soviet-led military alliance in Eastern Europe.
Suez Crisis demonstrates limits on British and French imperial freedom of action and the growing influence of the United States and Soviet Union.
Ghana becomes independent under Kwame Nkrumah, a landmark in sub-Saharan African decolonisation.
Sputnik 1, launched by the Soviet Union, begins the space age and intensifies the technology and prestige competition.
Cuban Revolution brings Fidel Castro’s movement to power; Cuba becomes central to Cold War politics in the Americas.
Congo Crisis follows independence from Belgium; foreign intervention, secession and the killing of Patrice Lumumba expose the vulnerabilities of decolonisation.
A large wave of African countries gains independence; the year is often called the “Year of Africa”, though decolonisation has different timelines across the continent.
Civil-rights, anti-apartheid, feminist, student, labour and anti-war movements expand across multiple societies, using distinct traditions and strategies.
Non-Aligned Movement takes shape around leaders including Jawaharlal Nehru, Gamal Abdel Nasser, Josip Broz Tito, Sukarno and Kwame Nkrumah; members do not always act as a unified bloc.
Berlin Wall is built, becoming a major symbol of the division of Europe.
Cuban Missile Crisis brings the United States and Soviet Union close to nuclear war; subsequent crisis management contributes to arms-control efforts.
Partial Test Ban Treaty restricts nuclear tests in the atmosphere, outer space and underwater.
US Civil Rights Act prohibits major forms of segregation and discrimination; activism and legal change continue beyond the statute.
Vietnam War escalates as US forces intervene heavily; Vietnamese, Laotian and Cambodian societies experience immense destruction and displacement.
China’s Cultural Revolution produces mass mobilisation, persecution, political turmoil and serious disruption to education and institutions.
Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is founded; regional cooperation develops amid Cold War divisions and economic change.
Six-Day War changes control of territory in the Middle East and deepens the Israeli–Palestinian conflict.
Prague Spring is suppressed by Warsaw Pact forces; student and labour protests occur in many countries, though with distinct causes and outcomes.
Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons is opened for signature; its nuclear disarmament, non-proliferation and peaceful-use pillars remain debated.
Apollo 11 lands humans on the Moon; the US achievement forms a landmark in the Space Race.
People’s Republic of China takes China’s seat at the United Nations, including the permanent Security Council seat.
Oil crisis reveals the global importance of energy supplies and reshapes inflation, industrial economies and geopolitical strategy.
Military coup in Chile overthrows Salvador Allende; dictatorship and human-rights abuses become part of the wider history of Cold War intervention in Latin America.
Carnation Revolution in Portugal leads to decolonisation of Portuguese African territories and contributes to political change in Portugal itself.

Fall of Saigon ends the Vietnam War in its conventional international framing; communist governments take power across Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia in the same period, though subsequent conflicts persist.
Helsinki Final Act addresses security, borders and human rights in Europe and becomes a reference point for dissident movements.
The Helsinki Final Act promotes principles of European security and human rights that later dissident movements use to challenge governments.
Camp David Accords and the Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty mark a major shift in Middle Eastern diplomacy.
Economic reform programme begins in China under Deng Xiaoping; market mechanisms and international economic integration expand over subsequent decades.
Iranian Revolution overthrows the Pahlavi monarchy and establishes the Islamic Republic.
Soviet invasion of Afghanistan begins a long war involving Afghan resistance, foreign support and massive displacement.
Debt crises and structural-adjustment policies affect many countries in the Global South; outcomes differ by country and remain contested.
Iran–Iraq War causes enormous casualties and destruction; the conflict ends without decisive territorial settlement.
Debt, commodity-price shocks and development policy disputes reshape economic and political debates across Latin America, Africa and other parts of the Global South.
Mikhail Gorbachev becomes Soviet leader and pursues perestroika and glasnost amid economic and political strain.
Chernobyl nuclear disaster exposes severe safety, environmental and governance failures in the Soviet system.
Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty is signed by the US and USSR, eliminating a category of ground-launched nuclear and conventional missiles.
Pro-democracy protests and state repression in Beijing centre on Tiananmen Square; the event remains politically sensitive and its history is contested in public memory.
Fall of the Berlin Wall becomes a symbol of the collapse of communist rule across much of Central and Eastern Europe.
German reunification takes place after the end of the Cold War division.
Dissolution of the Soviet Union ends the USSR; fifteen independent republics emerge, and the Cold War order is transformed.

t: Gulf War coalition expels Iraqi forces from Kuwait; the post-Cold War order is marked by US military predominance and continued regional instability.
The public Internet expands rapidly; e-mail, websites and digital networks transform communication, research, business and culture.
The end of apartheid negotiations accelerates in South Africa; Nelson Mandela is released in 1990 and constitutional transition continues into the early 1990s.
Maastricht Treaty is signed, laying the foundations for the European Union in its modern form.
United Nations Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro helps shape the global climate and sustainable-development agenda.
Rwandan genocide kills hundreds of thousands of Tutsi and moderate Hutu; international failure to prevent mass atrocity becomes a defining issue.
Apartheid ends as South Africa holds democratic elections and Nelson Mandela becomes president; transition follows decades of resistance and negotiation.
World Trade Organization is established, providing a central framework for multilateral trade rules.
The Dayton Accords end the Bosnian War; implementation, return of displaced people and accountability remain long-term issues.
Good Friday Agreement provides a framework for the Northern Ireland peace process; implementation and political tensions continue.
Nuclear tests by India and Pakistan intensify international debate on nuclear proliferation and regional security.
Euro is introduced as an accounting currency for participating EU members; euro banknotes and coins enter circulation in 2002.
The Kosovo War and NATO intervention intensify debates about humanitarian intervention, sovereignty and the use of force.
September 11 attacks in the United States kill nearly 3,000 people and lead to major changes in security policy and foreign intervention.
US-led intervention in Afghanistan removes the Taliban government from power initially; the conflict lasts two decades and ends with the Taliban’s return in 2021.
China joins the WTO, accelerating its integration into global trade and manufacturing networks.
The International Criminal Court is established under the Rome Statute entering into force; its reach depends on jurisdiction, cooperation and political realities.
US-led invasion of Iraq topples Saddam Hussein; occupation, insurgency, sectarian conflict and regional consequences continue for years.
Large EU enlargement brings many Central and Eastern European states into the Union, extending the post-Cold War European integration project.
Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami kill large numbers of people across countries bordering the ocean and lead to expanded regional disaster-warning cooperation.
Kyoto Protocol enters into force; climate diplomacy develops through successive negotiations, with disputes over responsibility, financing and targets.
Global financial crisis, following the collapse of major financial institutions and credit markets, produces recession, unemployment and new financial regulation debates.
Russia–Georgia war demonstrates continuing conflict over post-Soviet borders and security arrangements.
G20 leaders play an enlarged role in coordinating responses to the global financial crisis.
Social-media platforms play an increasingly central role in political communication, activism, misinformation and commercial data systems.
Arab Spring uprisings challenge authoritarian governments across parts of North Africa and West Asia; outcomes range from political transition to repression and civil war.
Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster follows an earthquake and tsunami in Japan; it renews global debates about nuclear safety and energy policy.
South Sudan becomes independent after a referendum; conflict and state-building challenges persist.
Syrian civil war leads to mass death, displacement and international intervention; it contributes to a wider regional humanitarian crisis.
China announces the Belt and Road Initiative, expanding infrastructure diplomacy and provoking debate over debt, connectivity and strategic influence.
Russia annexes Crimea after intervention and a disputed referendum; the action is widely rejected by the UN General Assembly and many states.
The Islamic State group captures territory in Iraq and Syria before losing its territorial caliphate; violence, forced displacement and counterterrorism operations affect the region.
UN member states adopt the 2030 Agenda and Sustainable Development Goals.
Paris Agreement is adopted under the UN climate process; it enters into force in 2016 and establishes a framework for nationally determined climate pledges.
The Iran nuclear agreement (JCPOA) is concluded between Iran and major powers; disputes over compliance and US withdrawal later weaken it.
Large-scale displacement from conflicts and persecution prompts political debate over refugees, borders, humanitarian protection and responsibility-sharing.
United Kingdom votes to leave the European Union; the referendum produces a prolonged political and legal process.
The Panama Papers expose offshore financial structures used by politicians, business leaders and wealthy individuals, prompting inquiries in multiple jurisdictions.
#MeToo becomes a global movement against sexual harassment and abuse, building on earlier activism and differing across countries.
Trade disputes between the United States and China intensify; tariffs and technology restrictions become features of strategic competition.
Large-scale protests in Hong Kong, Chile, Sudan and elsewhere show varied public demands about governance, rights, inequality and political representation.
COVID-19 is first identified in late 2019; the outbreak becomes a global pandemic in 2020.

t: Research cut-off for this edition. Contemporary events after this date are intentionally not projected as settled outcomes; revise the final section as reliable sources establish what happened.
The World Health Organization characterises COVID-19 as a pandemic; public-health measures, travel restrictions, healthcare pressures and economic disruption affect almost every region.
COVID-19 vaccines are developed, tested, authorised and deployed at unprecedented speed; access, safety communication, inequity and long-term effects become major public debates.
Global protests against racial injustice grow after the killing of George Floyd in the United States; movements reflect longer histories of policing, discrimination and colonial legacies.
The United Kingdom leaves the European Union’s single market and customs union at the end of the transition period, following Brexit.
Taliban forces return to power in Afghanistan after the withdrawal of US and allied forces; humanitarian and rights conditions, especially for women and girls, become major international concerns.
COP26 in Glasgow produces the Glasgow Climate Pact and renewed commitments, while countries continue to debate the pace and fairness of climate action.
Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February; the war drives displacement, sanctions, military support, energy shifts and renewed European security debate.
The global food and energy markets face severe disruption amid the war in Ukraine, sanctions, supply problems and climate-related shocks.
Generative AI systems become widely accessible to the public, triggering new debates about productivity, education, authorship, misinformation, labour and safety.
The World Health Organization ends the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency of International Concern designation; this does not mean the virus has disappeared or all impacts have ended.
The United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals reach the midpoint of their 2030 agenda; reports highlight uneven progress across countries and goals.

Hamas-led attacks in Israel and the subsequent Israeli military campaign in Gaza produce a major war and humanitarian catastrophe, with regional escalation and extensive international legal and diplomatic debate.
COP28 in Dubai concludes with a global stocktake and an agreement to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, alongside disputes about implementation and finance.
The Israel–Gaza war and regional escalation drive urgent diplomatic, humanitarian and legal debates; reported casualty figures and legal proceedings require dated updates.
Generative AI and advanced machine-learning systems expand rapidly in public services, research, business and education; governance, copyright, compute, labour and safety debates intensify.
COP29 in Baku produces a new climate-finance goal for developing countries, while disagreements continue over adequacy, responsibility and delivery.
The European Union adopts the AI Act, a major risk-based legal framework for artificial intelligence; phased implementation follows.
The 2024 Summer Olympic Games take place in Paris; global sport remains a cultural arena shaped by diplomacy, inequality and national identity.
Donald Trump begins a second term as president of the United States; changes in trade, climate, migration and foreign policy become major international developments.
The United Nations marks its 80th anniversary, reflecting on collective security, peacekeeping, human rights, development and the limitations of multilateral institutions.
COP30 takes place in Belém, Brazil, from 10–22 November; its outcome package includes climate-finance and adaptation decisions, while implementation and adequacy remain contested.
The International Year of Quantum Science and Technology is observed under the UN system, highlighting a century of quantum physics and its modern applications.
Major geopolitical tensions continue across Europe, the Middle East and parts of Asia; individual ceasefires and negotiations should be dated and re-checked because outcomes remain fluid.

The United States announces a large-scale military strike in Venezuela and reports the capture and removal of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores; legal, diplomatic and regional consequences continue to be contested and developing.
